 AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
 Photo: ed br / Pexels
 A report alleging chip sales to China and a fresh export rule put one of the AI trade's biggest winners under pressure
 by 
 John Chen

 Advanced Micro Devices lost nearly $100 billion in market value after a report alleged the company sold chips to China.
 AMD shares fell approximately 10.5% intraday on November 13, 2026. The drop erased around $100 billion in market capitalization, placing the chipmaker at the center of a wider retreat in AI semiconductor stocks.
 What sent AMD lower
 The trigger was a report alleging that AMD sold chips to China. For a company whose AI hardware sits under US export controls, that allegation goes straight to the question of compliance.
 AMD did not fall alone. The selloff was tied to a broader unwinding in AI chip stocks, driven by mounting concerns around rival Nvidia . Those concerns involve allegations that restricted chips were diverted to China.
 The link between the two companies is regulatory, not just reputational. AMD’s Instinct AI accelerators fall under the same export license regime as Nvidia’s chips. If Washington tightens the screws on one, the other feels it too.

 The China exposure in numbers
 Customers in China and Hong Kong accounted for 22.4% of AMD’s fiscal 2025 revenue. Singapore contributed about 12% more.
 That exposure became more pressing within days. The US Commerce Department introduced an interim final rule effective November 16, 2026. It requires licenses for shipments of advanced AI chips to five Southeast Asian countries.

 The rule also covers certain remote access arrangements that serve Chinese firms. Washington is trying to close routes that could let restricted computing power reach China indirectly, whether through physical shipments or access over the cloud.
 Strong numbers, complicated backdrop
 AMD reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% year over year. Its data-center revenue jumped 97%.
 The company guided fourth-quarter revenue to around $17 billion. That outlook now faces headwinds, including inventory issues and compliance risks linked to earlier restrictions on China.
 CEO Lisa Su has emphasized compliance with evolving regulations. She has also pointed out that China is critical across all of AMD’s segments: PC, gaming, and data center.
 AMD is exploring ways to cushion any shortfall in China revenue. One option involves leaning on older-generation chips that fall under existing licenses.
 What this means for AMD and the AI chip trade
 For investors, the key variable is not demand. AMD’s 45% revenue growth and 97% data-center expansion show demand is there. The open question is how much of that demand the company is legally allowed to serve, and where.
 The new Commerce Department rule is the first concrete test. How quickly AMD secures licenses for Southeast Asian shipments, and how often, will shape whether the fourth-quarter guidance of around $17 billion holds up.
 A report alleging chip sales to China is not a finding of wrongdoing. How that story develops, and whether regulators respond, could determine whether the selloff looks like an overreaction or an early warning.
